list.listitem: Suspect digoxin toxicity in patients taking digoxin who present with GI symptoms, visual changes, lethargy, confusion, weakness, or characteristic ECG changes ().
Initial assessment should include digoxin level, potassium, and ECG. Monitor renal function carefully.
Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (Fab) are the recommended treatment for life-threatening digoxin toxicity. B
Digoxin-specific Fab is 80% to 90% effective in reversing all signs and symptoms of digoxin toxicity. B
Activated charcoal, cholestyramine or colestipol may be helpful in reducing further digoxin exposure. C
Toxicity occurs in 2% to 5% of patients taking digoxin.

An estimated 1.0% of emergency department (ED) visits for adverse drug events were for digoxin toxicity among patients ≥40 years based on data from the National Electronic Injury Surveillance System–Cooperative Adverse Drug Event Surveillance project and the National Ambulatory (and Hospital Ambulatory) Medical Care Surveys (2005 to 2010). Among those over age 84 years, digoxin toxicity accounted for an estimated 3.3% (95% CI 2.3%–4.4%) of ED visits and 5.9% (95% CI, 4.0%–7.9%) of hospitalizations for all adverse drug events. Annual ED visits and hospitalizations remained fairly constant over those years.

In a population study of 1286 individuals in the Netherlands, only 0.04% of acute admissions were for digoxin intoxication; an incidence rate for digoxin intoxication-related admission of 48.5/100,000 prescriptions (95% CI 45.9, 51.2) or 1.94 admissions for intoxication per 1000 treatment-years. Women had a higher risk of digoxin intoxication than men (RR = 1.4; 95% CI 1.3, 1.6).

Using two population databases, the National Prescription Audit (2007-2014) and a national cohort of Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries (1999-2013), investigators found that prescriptions for digoxin decreased by 46.4%, from 8,099,856 to 4,343,735, and hospitalizations with digoxin toxicity as a principal or secondary diagnosis decreased dramatically from 15/100,000 person-years to 2/100,000 person-years.

Digoxin added to an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor in patients with and without diabetes who have heart failure and reduced ejection fraction, reduces heart failure hospitalization without substantial risk of toxicity. Digoxin toxicity was more common among patients with diabetes than without (6.5% vs. 5.8%), as was hospitalization for digoxin toxicity (1.4% vs. 0.8%).

Digoxin use in patients with heart failure who are in normal sinus rhythm is associated with lower rates of both hospitalization and clinical deterioration but not mortality; these data, however, are old and studies were completed before use of other therapeutic agents.
Digoxin increases the force of contraction of the heart by increasing cytosolic Ca2+ during systole. This is accomplished by inactivation of cardiomyocyte membrane Na+-K+-ATPase.
Toxic amounts of digoxin result in excessive elevation of intracellular Ca2+, which produces myocardial sensitization and predisposition to arrhythmias.

Digoxin also increases vagal tone to the sinoatrial (SA) and atrioventricular (AV) nodes, decreasing heart rate and conduction through the AV node. These changes manifest as the "digitalis effect" on ECG which is a scooping of the ST segment.

A person’s genetic profile influences the risk of cardiac digoxin toxicity. The ATP-binding cassette B1 gene (ABCB1) encodes P-glycoprotein, a transport protein important in digoxin bioavailability. Investigators in the Rotterdam population-based study found that, among digoxin users, variant alleles at each of the three loci in the ABCB1 gene were associated with an increased risk of sudden cardiac death compared with digoxin users with none or one T allele.
Renal insufficiency
Heart failure
Hypoxemia

Hypothyroidism
Age >80 years
Low lean body mass
Obtain history and objective proof, if possible, of the ingested amount of digoxin. Time since ingestion will aid in interpretation of digoxin concentrations.
Drugs that interact with digoxin include, but are not limited to:

Drugs that increase serum levels (amiodarone, benzodiazepines, bepridil, cyclosporine, diphenoxylate, indomethacin, itraconazole, macrolides, propafenone, propantheline, quinidine, quinine, spironolactone, tetracyclines, and verapamil). However, among 39,072 Ontarians taking digoxin who died suddenly, only 4.5% died within 14 days of receiving an antibiotic and there was no significant increase in the risk of sudden death following treatment with macrolide antibiotics relative to cefuroxime.

Drugs that decrease serum levels (aluminum/magnesium-containing antacids, antineoplastics, activated charcoal, cholestyramine, colestipol, kaolin/pectin, metoclopramide, neomycin, penicillamine, rifampin, St. John's Wort, and sulfasalazine).
Drugs that enhance pharmacodynamic effects (beta-blockers, calcium, diltiazem, diuretics, succinylcholine, sympathomimetics, and verapamil).
Drugs that antagonize pharmacodynamic effects, such as thyroid hormones.
Also ask about concomitant use of herbal cardiac glycosides (eg, oleander, foxglove or lily-of-the valley) and use of any medications that interact with digoxin.

Symptoms include ausea, anorexia or abdominal pain usually occurs first in 30% to 70%. Lethargy, confusion and weakness may also be present. In one case series in Spain of elderly subjects seen in the emergency department with digitalis toxicity, common reported symptoms were nausea (54.8%), fatigue (42.9%), vomiting (33.3%) and anorexia (28.6%). Almost half (47.5%) presented with bradycardia and most (87.8%) had an arrhythmia, most frequently atrial fibrillation.

Visual disturbances: hazy or blurred vision (common), flashing lights, halos, and green-yellow patterns (less common). In one case report, visual manifestations of digoxin toxicity were visual hallucinations and colored (yellow, green, blue and red) floaters.
Same symptoms as acute toxicity, but may be less obvious.
Order digoxin level, potassium, and ECG. Monitor renal function carefully.

Therapeutic range for treatment of heart failure is 0.5 to 0.9 ng/mL. In general, symptoms of digoxin toxicity are seen with concentrations greater than 2 ng/mL, measured 6 hours after ingestion. Toxicity can be seen at lower digoxin concentrations, however, in patients with co-existing hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, or hypothyroidism.

Concentration alone is not diagnostic and should always be interpreted in relation to the patient's clinical condition as there is a narrow margin between toxic and nontoxic concentrations. Concentrations measured within 6 hours of ingestion may be falsely elevated because the drug has not fully distributed.
Hyperkalemia (>5.0 mEq/L) indicates high concentrations of digoxin and also plays a role in prognosis.

ECG: bidirectional ventricular tachycardia (nearly diagnostic), new-onset Mobitz type I AV block, accelerated junctional rhythm with or without high-degree AV block, non-paroxysmal atrial tachycardia.
summarizes arrhythmias associated with digoxin toxicity. Ventricular dysrhythmias are more common in the elderly and supraventricular dysrhythmias are more common in children.

An Artificial Intelligence system has been developed for detection of digoxin toxicity based on ECG changes. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for the deep learning system was 0.912 in the validation cohort (84.6% sensitivity and 94.6% of specificity), and results were similar using only lead I (AUC = 0.960) vs. 12 leads (0.912).
Address the ABCs (airway, breathing, circulation).
Discontinue digoxin, prevent further exposure, and reduce absorption from the GI tract as initial steps (see secondary measures).
Emesis or lavage should not be routinely used due to limited efficacy.

Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (Fab) is the gold standard for treatment of life-threatening digoxin toxicity. It inactivates digoxin through binding to free digoxin and forming a digoxin-immune fragment complex which is excreted by the kidneys; Fab use will also correct hyperkalemia.

Digoxin-specific Fab is indicated in the following life-threatening situations:
Serum digoxin concentration >15 ng/mL at any time or >6 ng/mLin an adult or >4 ng/mL in a child 6 hours post ingestion. Acute ingestion >10 mg (adult) or >4 mg ( child). Potassium >5 mEq/L. Life-threatening arrhythmia. Chronic digoxin poisoning with arrhythmia, significant GI symptoms, or acute onset of significantly altered mental status or renal insufficiency.

Two digoxin-specific Fab formulations are available in the U.S.; Digibind® (38 mg/vial) and DigiFabTM (40 mg/mL).
Dosing can be based on serum digoxin concentration (SDC), amount ingested, or empirically dosed: SDC-based dosing: Dose (no. of vials) = [SDC (ng/mL) x Weight (kg)]/100. Consider giving 50% of calculated dose, then observing clinical impact and if no response in 1 to 2 hours administering the remainder of the dose. Ingestion-based dosing: Dose (no. of vials) = Total amount ingested (mg)/0.5 (each vial of either product will bind approximately 0.5 mg of digoxin). Empiric dosing: For acute poisoning of an adult or child, give 10 to 20 vials. For chronic poisoning of an adult give 3 to 6 vials and for chronic poisoning of a child give 1 to 2 vials.

Authors of a systematic review of 10 case series (there are no randomized trials) suggest that full neutralizing doses are unnecessary in most cases as drug binding is highly effective and digoxin bioavailability is 60% to 80%, making calculated digoxin-Fab doses overestimates. They recommend full doses primarily for patients with imminent cardiac failure, but otherwise suggest a small 80 mg bolus (2 vials), repeated if necessary, titrated against clinical effect for acute poisoning and a single vial for patients with chronic poisoning, repeated after 1 hour if no response.

There have been no reports of acute hypersensitivity or anaphylaxis with digoxin-specific Fab to date. Hypokalemia has rarely occurred. Patients with allergies to papain, chymopapain, or other papaya extracts may be at risk because trace amounts of these residues may remain in the preparation.

There were 78 reports for DigiBind and 43 reports for DigiFab submitted post-marketing to the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System through Dec 2019. The most frequently reported adverse events for both products [DigiBind and DigiFab, respectively] were cardiac (bradycardia [3.8% and 3.9%], cardiac arrest [3.3% and 3.9%], and hypotension [2.4% and 2.6%]) and non-cardiac (nausea [1.9% and 2.6%] and hyperkalemia [1.4% and 1.9%]). No deaths were attributed to the medications.

is a clinical decision making tool for the use of digoxin-specific Fab in non-life-threatening toxicity (defined as the absence of life-threatening situations). If it is not cost effective, do not administer digoxin-specific Fab. Observe the patient and consider activated charcoal and/or resin (cholestyramine or colestipol).

Patients with chronic digoxin toxicity may be less likely to benefit from digoxin-specific Fab. In one case series of 128 patients admitted with digoxin toxicity without ventricular arrythmias, 78 (61%) initially received digoxin-specific Fab (median dose 1.5 vials) and the remainder received supportive care. There were no significant differences in deaths (12% vs. 14% in those treated with supportive care), hospital length of stay (median 6 days in both groups), or mean changes in heart rate or serum potassium within 4 hours. Patients receiving Fab had significantly lower initial blood pressures but there were no differences in digoxin concentrations (4.4 nmol/L [range: 3.3-9] vs. 4.2 [range: 2-11.2], respectively) or serum potassium concentrations (5.4 mmol/L [range: 3-11] vs. 5.1 mmol/L [range: 3.5-8.2], respectively).

Activated charcoal, cholestyramine or colestipol bind digoxin in the gut, reduce exposure, and may be beneficial in purposeful overdoses where elevated quantities of digoxin are seen in the intestine. Contact a poison center before administering activated charcoal for appropriate recommendations. Activated charcoal should not be administered to patients who are at risk for aspiration or when gut motility is absent.

If digoxin-specific Fab is not immediately available, phenytoin (100 mg IV bolus repeated every 5 minutes, maximum 1000 mg in adults; 15-20 mg/kg in a child) or lidocaine (1.0-1.5 mg/kg IV bolus followed by continuous infusion at 1-4 mg/min in adults; 1.0-1.5 mg/kg IV bolus followed by 30-50 μg/kg/min in a child) may be used to treat ventricular arrhythmias.
IV atropine (0.5 mg adult; 0.02 mg/kg child) repeated every 5 minutes may be used to treat supraventricular bradyarrhythmias or high degree, symptomatic AV block.

Pacing and cardioversion are of limited use and class IA antiarrhythmics (quinidine, procainamide, and disopyramide) should not be used as they may induce or worsen AV nodal block, although use in the setting of digoxin toxicity has not been studied.
Administration of calcium prior to digoxin-specific Fab may exacerbate arrhythmias.
Extracorporeal treatment is not indicated for digoxin toxicity or for removal of digoxin-Fab complex.

Continuous venovenous hemodialysis alone was effective in a case report of a woman with digoxin toxicity and severe acute kidney injury. Hemodialysis was used due to hypervolemia, hyperkalemia, and cardiac instability and also resulted in decreased digoxin levels and recovery.
Diligent monitoring of renal function for patients taking digoxin.
Educate patients so they recognize symptoms of digoxin toxicity, and to always consult with physician or pharmacist before starting or stopping any prescription or non-prescription medication.
Limit prescribing of digoxin to patients where benefits clearly outweigh risks (much fewer good indications than previously).
Digoxin should not be used in patients with low ejection fraction, sinus rhythm, and no history of HF symptoms where the risk of harm is not balanced by any known benefit.
Prevent hypokalemia; low potassium concentrations may lead to digoxin toxicity.

Initiate therapy with digoxin 0.125 mg/day and if possible use computerized drug ordering that provides drug–drug interactions, monitoring of renal function, electrolyte levels, and digoxin concentrations.
Digoxin concentrations will increase, up to 30-fold, after digoxin-specific Fab is administered and should not be used to guide subsequent therapy.
Continuous monitoring of ECG, electrolytes and clinical symptoms of digoxin toxicity.

The following are indications for routine measurement of serum digoxin concentrations:
Following initial dosing. Patients with changing or impaired renal function. Not experiencing adequate clinical response. Ascertaining patient adherence. Receiving potentially interacting medications. Prevention and diagnosis of toxicity.
Potassium greater than 5.5 mEq/dL is associated with 100% mortality.

In a retrospective review of 171 cases of digoxin poisoning in 4 emergency departments in Spain from 2013-2015, 30-day mortality was 3 of 7 patients (43%) with acute poisoning and 20 of 164 (12.1%) with chronic poisoning.

In-hospital and 30-day mortality rates associated with digoxin toxicity decreased significantly from 6.0% (95% confidence interval [CI] 5.2-6.8) to 3.7% (95% CI 2.2-5.7) and from 14.0% (95% CI 13.0-15.2) to 10.1% (95% CI 7.6-13.0), respectively, using two population databases - the National Prescription Audit (2007-2014) and a national cohort of Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries (1999-2013).
Mortality due to digoxin toxicity is a function of age and degree of toxicity: Age >60 years: 58%. Age 40 to 50 years: 34%. Age <40 years: 8%.13 SDC >6 ng/mL: 50% mortaility.

Digoxin-specific Fab is 80 % to 90% effective in reversing all signs and symptoms of digoxin toxicity. In one case series of 36 patients with digoxin toxicity, digoxin-specific Fab was highly effective in binding free digoxin and resolving gastrointestinal symptoms, but the effect on heart rate was only moderate (mean change 8 beats/min); this was likely due to other concomitant medications (eg, beta blockers) and underlying co-morbidities.
Most patients will show clinical improvement by 1 hour after treatment and complete response by 4 hours.
Appropriate treatment may decrease hospital stay by 1.5 days.

In a case series of 13 neonates with toxic digoxin levels (>2 ng/ml), only 3 were symptomatic and all three had plasma digoxin levels >5 ng/ml. Symptoms were GI and central nervous system. Two premature neonates were treated with DigiFabTM, and hypokalemia developed in both.
